key_insight: Functional septorhinoplasty was associated with measurable changes in higher-order olfactory brain activity in persistent COVID-19-related smell dysfunction, suggesting central neural plasticity alongside improved airflow.
clinical_relevance: This study suggests that restoring nasal airflow may help modulate brain network responses involved in smell, offering a potential mechanistic basis for symptom improvement in selected patients.
method: Prospective cohort study with persistent COVID-19-related olfactory dysfunction patients
Psychophysical olfactory testing, nasal airflow measurements, and task-based fMRI before and 6 months after surgery
Whole-brain analysis correlated neural activation changes with clinical and airflow measures
evidence_signal: In 8 participants with paired scans, baseline and post-operative fMRI showed region-specific activation/deactivation changes, with several correlations to nasal airflow and olfactory scores.
watch_item: Very small sample size and lack of a control group limit certainty about causality and generalizability.
paper_title: Functional plasticity of the olfactory network following functional septorhinoplasty in persistent COVID-19-related olfactory dysfunction: an fMRI study
